lesson:
The AI project cycle is a framework consisting of a sequence of six stages designed to tackle artificial intelligence challenges: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modeling, evaluation, and deployment. Visually, a project flows sequentially from problem scoping to the final deployed AI solution.

Problem scoping is the most important step in the AI project cycle because it determines how success is defined for the project, allowing teams to start with the end in mind. To ensure completeness, the four Ws prompt is used: Who, What, Where, and Why. "Who" identifies the stakeholders, beneficiaries, or those most concerned with the challenge, such as bus drivers and passengers in a bus safety scenario. "What" explores the nature of the problem and how it is known to exist, such as drivers being drowsy and leading to road accidents based on statistical evidence. "Where" looks at the context or the time perspective in which the problem arises, such as a bus driver being unwell or drowsy. "Why" defines the motivation and value proposition, such as improving safety and decreasing the probability of accidents for drivers and passengers.

Data acquisition involves finding and collecting the appropriate data needed for an AI solution. Data can come from origin sources like active e-commerce websites, or from public domain sources and organizations made available as input for AI problems. Examples of data sources include Kaggle, which is a platform for data scientists and machine learning engineers to publish datasets, find datasets, and build models; Amazon Web Services (AWS), which offers a registry of open data; the World Bank, which provides national and international data on health, education, and nutrition; and the United States government, which provides population datasets.

Data exploration is the data science aspect where the dataset is viewed from different perspectives to determine how it can best be used to solve the problem. Because raw numbers and datasets can be overwhelming, human-friendly visualization tools such as Power BI and Tableau are generally used to transform raw numbers into charts, graphs, and aggregate views that help humans identify patterns and big picture characteristics.

Modeling is the heavy lifting phase where a mathematical algorithm or program is created based on input data to interact with new, unseen data and yield the best results. AI is the larger organizing concept, with machine learning inside it, and deep learning inside machine learning. AI mimics human intelligence, machine learning enables machines to improve with experience, and deep learning trains on vast amounts of data. In this context, feeding data into a model is analogous to accelerated experience. Machine learning modeling techniques are categorized into three main families: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning determines relationships through training on known labeled data, where every data point is categorized into a class associated with a fixed mark by a human. Sub-techniques of supervised learning include classification, which deals with categorical (qualitative) data to predict a class or category (such as student grades or fox identification), and regression, which deals with numerical (quantitative) data to predict a numerical measurement (such as housing prices or future student marks). Unsupervised learning involves a machine discovering patterns and correlations by traversing large amounts of unlabeled data without human supervision, grouping similar-looking data together. A common unsupervised technique is clustering, such as K-means clustering, which groups unlabeled data into clusters (like separating shadows of wildlife into animals and birds). Reinforcement learning relies on the machine receiving rewards based on actions to understand success.

Evaluation is stage five, where a mechanism is used to judge, score, or evaluate the quality and behavior of the created model. Each modeling approach has a corresponding evaluation technique: classification problems use accuracy and the confusion matrix; regression problems use root mean square error; and clustering problems use the silhouette method.

Deployment is the final stage where a high-quality model is put into meaningful use in the real world, moving from a lab setting into production to solve real-world problems. Deployment can occur via various platforms such as mobile applications, websites, or cloud servers, allowing actual people to take advantage of the work done.
